utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Is it Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness make the solemn declaration first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good afternoon. According to the ruling of the Trial Chamber, I will just introduce the witness to the Trial Chamber, and after that I believe that Mr. Pantelic will cross-examine him, and then the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Erletic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Can you hear well? Can you hear through the headset?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, for the Trial Chamber, would you tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: My name is Jovan Erletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Erletic, during the deposition hearings in Belgrade, you have already testified. It is the decision of the Trial Chamber that your cross-examination be continued here at the Tribunal in The Hague. Therefore, I would like to remind you of everything you have been told about the manner of testifying. Would you please pause between question and answer. You will first be examined by Mr. Pantelic, and then the Prosecutor will have the right to additional cross-examination. If necessary, we, as the Defence of Mr. Zaric, who have called you as a witness, will also have the right to examine you in case there is anything we need to clarify after your cross-examination by the other Defence counsel and the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That would be it, and I believe that Mr. Pantelic will start now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Erletic. We have already met. We met in Belgrade. And we know each other indirectly through my investigator, who had a brief interview with you in 2001. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Erletic, on page 194 of the transcript from Belgrade, you mentioned that the meeting at the command, and we are now discussing the document entitled "Information," that this meeting was attended by officers of the East Bosnia Corps of the army of Republika Srpska. You mentioned Colonel Jakovljevic, who was the security organ in the corps, and Colonel Dosen, who was the assistant commander for morale and other affairs in the corps. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For the record, would you tell us whether you remember Colonel Jakovljevic's first name, for the sake of the record? If you can remember it.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the first name of Colonel Dosen?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I only knew them by their last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the East Bosnia Corps at the time was and what his rank was?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: At that time, the commander was Novica Simic, and I think he had the rank of lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me now, Mr. Erletic: Quite a few years have elapsed. We all agree about that. But do you remember in the debate between the representatives of the civilian authorities and the military organs at that meeting, which was also attended by Blagoje Simic, how did Dr. Simic behave? What was his standpoint? What impression did he make? What do you know about this personally?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain that. At that meeting, Dr. Simic behaved very correctly, very properly. He was calm, quiet. And when there was a heated debate, he tried to calm it down. That's what I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At that discussion, can you describe the behaviour of the other participants? And I'm referring primarily to Stevan Todorovic, Milan Simic, and Mr. Minic, from the MUP of Republika Srpska, the police ministry of Republika Srpska. Were they also calm?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: During my testimony in Belgrade, I said that I didn't know this gentleman, the representative of the SUP. I don't even know his name. I didn't even try to get acquainted with him, because of the way he behaved. I think that everything that happened at that meeting, and the debate was quite harsh, but this was by Stevan Todorovic and the representative of the SUP, whom I don't know and whom I don't want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And just a few questions, Mr. Erletic, about the sequence of events in that period of time. Are you aware of the fact that around the second half of November or the end of November, Stevan Todorovic and Milan Simic were arrested by members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I know they were arrested, but it was not by the police of our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After this event, because the information bears the date of the 1st of December, 1992, after this event, did any information follow, if I might remind you, and this information contain something about the arrest. Can we agree on that, that information followed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: As far as the time sequence goes, yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know, further, that in December 1992 legal proceedings were initiated before the military court in Banja Luka against Lugar and other volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Erletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Erletic. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Good day. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You understand I'm going to ask you a few more questions about your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your depositions evidence in Belgrade, you said that you lived in Pelagicevo. Can you just tell us briefly the period when you lived in Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I lived in Pelagicevo from my date of birth, the 2nd of September, 1952 [as interpreted], and I was absent only in 1971 and 1972, when I served in the JNA. Then from 1973 to 1976, and in mid-1977, I worked in Samac, because that's where I worked. And from 1978 until today, I have been living in Pelagicevo. Sabac, not Samac, but Sabac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and one more correction on line 5, page 22, it's 1951. That's when the witness was born, in 1951, not 1952.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for the corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You gave evidence in Belgrade about your military service. What I want to ask you about is your position in 1991 and up until April 1992, in relation to the military. Were you in the reserve or were you in a military unit between the beginning of 1991 and mid-April 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: In the second half of April 1992, as a reserve officer, I was called up and appointed company leader of the military police in the Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the -- any of the detachments attached to the 17th Tactical Group, that is, the 1st or 2nd or 3rd or 4th Detachments of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: No, I did not belong to any detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you tell us the date in April 1992 when you were called up and appointed a company leader of the military police in the Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I don't have a good head for dates, and this was ten years ago. But I do know that it was in the second half of April, between the 20th and the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you in the reserve between January 1991 and the date you were appointed to the military police in April 1992? And if so, did you engage in training exercises in that 16-month period?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: No, I did not engage in any kind of training exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence in -- I'm sorry. I'll just take you back to the question. The question was: Were you in the reserve in those dates? And I think in Belgrade you told us that you were in the reserve forces of the state security detachment in Brcko. Does that jog your memory about your military -- your personal military status in 1991 up until mid-April 1992? That's at page 197.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember well what I said, and I abide by what I said. As a member of the reserves, if you understood me correctly, I was not active, nor was I activated. I was simply part of the reserve force under the state security service in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you ever activated to perform any work in the state security work after the outbreak of the war? That's in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did your role as the -- as a commander in the military police from mid-April 1992 involve, and until when did you perform that role? Two questions there. What I'm asking you is: What did you do, and until when?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: When I was appointed company leader in the military police, it was a small unit I was in charge of, some 20 or so policemen, and I remained at that post for a very brief period of time, until the JNA left. And when the 2nd Posavina Brigade was formed, I was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is your role in military police. You said it was attached to the 17th Tactical Group. Was it attached to the -- were you attached to the command under Colonel Nikolic of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: As a military police commander, I did not belong to the command of the 17th Tactical Group. It was the security officer who was my direct superior who was part of the command, and the second superior was, of course, the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was the person who you reported to, or who was your superior when you were the commander for military police?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: My superior was Maksim Simeunovic, and the commander was Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was this responsibility for military police in relation to the entirety of the 17th Tactical Group or apart of it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the command of the 17th Tactical Group had a military police company under its command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm trying to find out is exactly what you did and where you fitted in and what the military police did. Can you briefly explain that to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain. The headquarters was in Pelagicevo, and there was a small number of policemen guarding the command headquarters and parts of roads and the military depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Military police entrusted with the investigations of -- the investigation into alleged criminal activity by soldiers, aren't they, and the disciplining of -- or the keeping of discipline in the military, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: No. No. That was done by the security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you involved in the moving of prisoners from the TO in Bosanski Samac in late April 1992 and then transferred to JNA facilities in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: No. The military police didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you a member of a political party in 1991, 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Ever since I was born, I was never a member of any party, and I'm still not a member of a party.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you on the night of the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: On the night of the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992, I was at home. It was at my home. It was my own personal house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying you were mobilised or called up after the Serbian takeovers in Bosanski Samac municipality on the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I told you: As far as I remember, between the 20th and the 25th, I was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is: You said earlier that you were a little bit unsure about dates and that's quite understandable so long ago. I'm just trying to link it to an event. Was it before or after the takeover that you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I had only heard that there was a takeover in Samac, and I was mobilised afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you involved in the collecting of weapons from people in the municipality of Bosanski Samac after the takeover, the days immediately after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: No. The military police did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In the document which the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, of which you were number 4, signed, on the 1st of December, 1992, that's P127 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could be shown the document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's P127. While it's coming, I'll ask the question:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In this document -- you're familiar with the document, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness is nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're nodding. Can you just answer verbally for us, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the document. And I talked about this document in Belgrade while I gave my statement. But at the time, I was not the commander of the military police. At the time, I worked in the technical service, working for the 2nd Posavina Brigade. And since at the time we did not have an assistant commander for the logistics, I was carrying out his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have you got the version in B/C/S there? I just want to take you to the first page, Mr. Erletic. Do you have the version in your own language there, Mr. Erletic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to take you to the second paragraph, or the one that starts: "First, it is a fact that the 17th Tactical Command played a significant role." Can you see that paragraph? It should be about halfway or a third to halfway along the front page. It will be on the first page. I think you'll find it in the second paragraph, under "report."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have you -- can you just read that paragraph to yourself, the one that starts: "First, it is a fact that the 17th Tactical Command." And perhaps if you could also read the next paragraph, which also says "second." If you could just read those to yourself for a moment, because I just want to ask you a few questions about them. You're nodding. That means you've read it to your self?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember in Belgrade I asked you about the report and your answer was that all that was contained in that report is true? I just want to ask you about something in the first paragraph, about the significant role in the pre-war period. What can you tell the Trial Chamber -- this is my question: What can you tell the Trial Chamber about the significant role of the 17th Tactical Group in the pre-war period and the first days of the war in the territorial organisation of the several detachments in Samac municipality, the organised arming of the Serbian people in particular, and the provision of proper combat tactics and equipment for the armed struggle in the region? I just want you to elaborate on that a little, if you can, to the Trial Chamber, and just expand upon that significant role for us.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I remember very well that I told you, in Belgrade, that I was never involved in politics. I never did anything that I wasn't supposed to do. I only always did my job. I was an athlete and I was a hunter. I never played any role in politics. I was never involved in politics. I did not -- I was not interested in politics either, and I only did my job. That is exactly what I told you in Belgrade. I also remember telling you in Belgrade that everything that has to do with my involvement and the work I was carrying out, I can explain everything with regard to that. With regard to this information, however, I said, loudly and clearly, that the information was signed, and I have signed it as well, because at the command we had decided that these actions were not good for the morale of soldiers, because we wanted to let them know that the soldiers were not carrying out these actions, that it was done by somebody else, and this is the reason why we had signed this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All I want to know is if you can expand upon anything that's written here, just from your knowledge of what you saw and one of the signatories of this document. If you can't, that's perfectly okay. So I just move to the second paragraph, where it refers to the arrival of a group of so-called "Serbian commandos," led by Crni and Debeli, in a helicopter. It says: "Nikolic and the 17th Tactical Group command initially branded it as a `paramilitary group' and a `group of bandits and mercenaries,' but after only five or six days they endorsed it and explained it as a `legal elite unite of Serbian commandos' whose arrival had been legalised through the official organs of government and the army, both at the level of Samac municipality and at the highest level in Serbia and Yugoslavia." What I simply want to ask you, and if you don't know, that's fine, but can you tell the Trial Chamber anything about, firstly, the arrival of these Serbian commandos or the paramilitaries, and secondly, about Colonel Nikolic and the 17th Tactical Group's command -- Tactical Group command's endorsement of this group after a few days? You follow the two questions that I -- that I'm asking you? Can you tell us anything else about the paramilitaries, their arrival, or -- and/or the endorsement or their endorsement by the command of the 17th Tactical Group and Colonel Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything about it, because at the time I was not active and I was not within the command of the 17th Tactical Group either. I had heard, however, from some people that they had arrived, as you say, by helicopter, but I have not seen that myself. I noticed them on the streets and in other places, but who organised this, who brought them in, how it all happened, I really don't know, because I was not an eyewitness and I can only tell you what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you noticed them on the street. Did you notice them on the street before you were called back into the military police between April 20th and 25th?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And where did you see them when you noticed them on the streets?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw them in Pelagicevo, Pelagicevo, where I lived, and this is where the command was. Two hundred to three hundred metres away from my family house in which I lived was the command, and this is where I noticed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying you noticed them at the command or somewhere else in Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I noticed them at the centre of Pelagicevo. That's about 150 metres away from the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they doing in the centre of Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: In the centre of Pelagicevo, there was a cafe, and everybody liked to gather in that cafe. I noticed them in front of the cafe, and also I noticed them inside, sitting in the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what was it that led you to notice them?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I noticed them because they were not from our territory. They were dressed differently. They were also made up in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they wearing that was different, and what do you mean by "made up in a different way"?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: At the time, the JNA army wore the same outfits. It was beige. That's what their uniforms were like. However, these men wore camouflage uniforms, and this is what differentiated them from the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you find out who they were?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Well, you know how it is when you're at a cafe. If you don't know what goes on in a city, or especially in a village, you go to have a drink at the cafe, and this is where you find out what goes on around you. That's the best way to find out what is going on, the best source.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what did you find out about who these people were and why they were there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: At the time, I found out that they had come from outside. They had landed in a helicopter in Batkusa, and the helicopter landed on the stadium. That's all what we knew, what people knew, what a simple man could know at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were these people staying when you saw them in the centre of Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: You mean when they were staying as in spending their time?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were they being accommodated, that is, sleeping and eating?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were sleeping on the stadium in Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many times do you remember seeing them in Pelagicevo or around before you were called up into the military police again?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: To be very honest with you, at the time, people were not really moving about a lot. The communication was not great either. I only noticed them because I was at the cafe and around the cafe. But they were visible. We would see them every day, on a daily basis, one of them would be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were people saying -- people in Pelagicevo, where you were living, were they saying anything about the conduct or behaviour of these paramilitaries? That's before you were called up into the army.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that people were not talking about them a lot, for the simple reason that people were afraid of them, and this is why we were even avoiding that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Also in the document, that's P127, on that same page, it refers to the group playing "an indisputably positive role in the liberation of Samac, as a part of the special battalion in fighting at Vidovica, Kornica, Garevac, and Kladari." I apologise if my pronunciation is not too good, "in the liberation of the corridor to Brcko and in other operations." Did you participate in any of those operations? That's Vidovica or Brcko -- sorry, Kornica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Also in the document, it refers to, over the page, where it says "fifth," I'll just read it to you. If you can find the paragraph -- it starts off with "fifth." It says "second, third, fourth, fifth." Every paragraph has a different number. The second or third line says: "With the blessing of those who had brought them in and those who had sent them they engaged in unheard of looting of private and socially owned property." What I simply ask you is this, in your own experience and as a signatory to this document, what do you know or what did you see of the looting by these Serbian commandos in the area?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was working in the technical department, and I was also the assistant commander for logistics [as interpreted]. From all the units, men working in the logistics had to come and see me, to report to me. They had to do so because we were issuing food, uniforms, and so on and so forth. So from the areas they were coming from, they were bringing information. They were saying: Such-and-such a person was beaten up. Another person was beaten up. A vehicle was taken from a person, stolen. There was looting, and so on and so forth. And this is what I heard in my office from these men. However, during the meetings of the command of the brigade, we heard other information coming from other areas, and this is how we came to the conclusion that such actions were going on, and this is why we drafted this information. I signed this information because I heard from the men working with me, and also from other superiors at the command who had seen these things. I personally did not see any of these actions, because I was in my office and not on the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. I just got an information from my client that he would need to leave this courtroom for about 10 minutes, if you'd allow him to leave. He wishes the proceedings to go on, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, he can leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And one very small clarification for the transcript, on page 16, line 8. Mr. Erletic had said I was acting assistant commander for logistics, not assistant commander. Just this clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just to clarify something from your answer, Mr. Erletic. You just told us about soldiers coming to you and saying such-and-such a person was beaten up, a vehicle was taken from a person, stolen, et cetera. In all the things you just referred to a moment ago, you were referring, weren't you, to your soldiers or troops telling you about what the paramilitaries from Serbia were doing? I'm just trying to clarify your answer.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic asked you about the meeting which was between the civilian authorities and the command of the 17th -- sorry, the 2nd Posavina Brigade in relation to the document in front of you. You said that Mr. Simic or Dr. Simic behaved correctly or behaved properly and tried to calm it down. You're giving your evidence --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- over ten and a half years, almost ten and a half years since the meeting occurred. You didn't take any notes of the meeting, did you, or what was said there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when you're giving your evidence today, is it true that you -- or fair to say that you don't have a very, very good memory of who said what at the meeting, but you're left with an impression of Dr. Simic being calm and behaving correctly and other people being more aggressive, but you can't really remember the precise words that anyone used?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I will clarify a little. I cannot recall exactly what people said. That's true. But I can remember how Dr. Simic behaved. I can remember that. And this is why. I'll explain. This person was the representative of the police. When he was behaving aggressively and when he threatened that he would put us in prison, I was the one who reacted. I was the person who reacted, and perhaps in a vulgar way, I resisted him. And I told him that he couldn't do this, that we wouldn't allow this to happen, and so on. And before that, and before that, Mr. Simic was calm, had a calm appearance. He tried to calm things down, and after that as well, and that's precisely because -- I remember this because I was one of the people who reacted a little more heatedly and spoke to this gentleman who was the representative of the police. That is precisely what I remember, and why I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But you remember Dr. Simic as being a participant in the meeting, that is, the document being discussed, different people from the two groups, the civilian authorities and the military, discussing the contents of the document and each putting their views forward, but Dr. Simic expressed his views in a calmer way than other people?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: My impression was, looking at the behaviour of Dr. Simic, that he had come to be calm, to be calm, to overcome the problems so that there shouldn't be any dangerous things happening, there shouldn't be any ill effect. That was my impression of his behaviour. But the main culprits why this discussion and argument happened between the command and them, in my opinion, the culprits were Stevan Todorovic and the representative of the police. This person that I did not meet and the person I never want to meet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Did not know, interpreter's correction, and the person I never want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you about is your impression is that Dr. Simic was certainly aware of the report and its contents, and he, along with the others, discussed it, but the arguments or the -- I'm sorry. I withdraw the word "arguments," but the aggression came from other people?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, and if you've understood me correctly, this meeting I got the impression that Dr. Simic calmly, with a cool head, came to the meeting in order to overcome the problems. That was the sense of it. So that there would be no heated discussion that did happen, so that this meeting wouldn't -- the people wouldn't leave this meeting the way they did leave this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Re. I apologise for interrupting. I wonder, just for the sake of clarity, Mr. Erletic: It says in the transcript, on page 19, lines 4 to 6 - this is one of your answers - and it says -- this is lines 4 to 6, as I say, page 19. You say: "In my opinion, the culprits were Stevan Todorovic and the representative of the police. This person that I did not meet and the person I never want to meet."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Judge Mumba has just said to me that the interpreter then interprets what you've said and explains it. So disregard the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Dr. Simic said something to the meeting along the lines of being offended by the allegations made in this document, very serious ones, about criminality by the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, of which he was the president?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I told you, and I'm trying to tell you everything I know to help clarify this and find the real truth. I'm telling you again: I cannot recall the details about what -- who said what exactly, because a lot of time has elapsed. And this was not the field of my work at the time. But I remember these details the way they occurred because I had perhaps been one of the culprits why this meeting happened noisily, or more noisily than it should have happened, because I intervened when the representative of the police said that he would be putting people in prison and punishing people. I was the one who resisted him, who opposed him. And probably you will think that that was rather rude of me, but at the time I was in a state to oppose him physically. That's the reason why I remember this detail that I told you about now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I just ask you again about the impression of Dr. Simic's awareness, I'm not meaning the exact words that were said, but I'm asking you -- you certainly -- look, I suggest you had the impression because of Dr. Simic's participation in the meeting that he had read the report and was aware of the contents and the very serious allegations that the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade was making against the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, on the basis that -- well, it's maybe third or fourth time that my learned friend is calling this witness to speculate. What was in the head of the -- of Dr. Simic, whether he read that or not, whether he discussed or not. And this witness several times give the answer. I don't know how long we shall going to listen this one-way discussion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I've asked the question several times because I'm still trying to get an answer to that part of the question and it's only based upon the witness's impression, based on Dr. Simic's participation, whether he gained that impression. That's all. And I haven't quite got the answer. The witness can answer it any way, yes, no, I don't know, or whatever. But he hasn't answered that specific part. That's why I've asked it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness has stated what happened, as far as he can remember, regarding Dr. Simic's participation. But since you feel it is an important part of your case, you can proceed and press the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do apologise to my learned friend. Maybe that would be a proper suggestion, to formulate the question: What is your personal knowledge about the topic that Mr. -- Dr. Simic discussed or whether he expressed himself that he knew something about this information, in that line. Otherwise it's too general questions that are driving us nowhere. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Erletic, I'm asking you about your impression, based upon yours and Dr. Simic's, and everyone else's participation in the meeting. Did you get the impression that Dr. Simic had read and understood the contents of the report? I'm not asking you for exact words, but just from everything you saw at the meeting, is that the impression that you gained, that he was familiar with the report, maybe from things he said or your memory of it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I cannot claim now whether Mr. Simic had read the report -- the information. But what I do recall and what I do recall well, and if I can remember that and make an assessment, I think that some of the individuals who had come to the meeting had come -- when they were intoxicated somewhat, and these were the representatives of the police, of the MUP, as it was called then. While Mr. Simic at the meeting appeared calm. That's how I saw him. He was normal, if I say that. He came to talk, to negotiate, so that there would be an agreement out of the meeting, coming out of the meeting. But in my opinion - and I am -- work in the catering and I've been in catering for 25 years - the other two gentlemen who were there, and one of them is Stevan Todorovic, and the other person's name I don't know, and even if I did know his name, I wouldn't utter it, they were intoxicated. So the meeting didn't take very long. There was an argument between this gentleman and myself. That was the first thing that happened, before any kind of discussion took place, the discussion that should have happened and why the meeting was called in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You don't remember Dr. Simic denying the contents of the report, saying this isn't true, this didn't happen, this is rubbish?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I told you that I cannot remember the details, because that was ten years ago from that. And I did not know that this would happen so that I would try and remember who said what. I told you why I remember that one detail. I remembered it because I was one of the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you aware, or did you participate in any joint actions with the police or paramilitaries or the Serbian commandos and the JNA or VRS? I mean military operations.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Any party wishing to ask questions arising out of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Erletic, now there was a lot of discussion regarding this document and the atmosphere at the meeting, and I'd just like you to make a clarification regarding this, please. Do you have any personal knowledge what Stevan Todorovic and certain other policemen under his command in Samac did in 1992 and 1993? Did you see anything personally? Did you hear anything about what he did?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago: Where I was not -- what I did not take part of, I cannot stand by. I heard things, what was happening, kidnapping, smuggling, certain people were beaten up. I heard about that, and I heard about that from those soldiers and the officers who were under me and who came to me. Personally, I did not see anything anywhere. I was not in the position to see anything, because I was sitting in an office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Erletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Erletic. I'm just going to ask you a couple of questions. First of all, this is with respect to your testimony here today. Can you tell me, please: Since when have you known Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I've known Simo Zaric since he came to the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And can you remember, Mr. Erletic, when that was?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, but I think this was in the second half of 1992, approximately. I cannot tell you precisely, but perhaps October/November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that the information that you and the command adopted was prepared in October and November 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I know that it was spoken at the command that this was being prepared, that this was worked on, that units were visited, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Erletic, when did you come to the post of the commander of the company of military police, as you said, the end of April, 1992, and this company was attached to the command of the 17th Tactical Group, do you know whether the detachments that at the time were part of the 17th Tactical Group, they had their own squads of military police?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Erletic, you mention here that you were a member of a squad for defence preparations, SDB, that is, detachment of the state security service in Brcko. That is not contested; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: That was a reserve squad of the state security service; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you, as members of that squad, did you have any kind of meetings?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: If I may clarify somewhat with respect to that squad. This squad was a detachment of the state security service, and that was detachment in Brcko. And it was a multi-ethnic squad. When shooting started, when all this started happening, this squad was disbanded, so it didn't exist any more. That's why I was deactivated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I was just going to ask you: Who were the members of the squad? But since you've answered that this squad was a multi-ethnic squad, I was interested in the methods of the work. You, while this squad was in existence, did you have any meetings at detachment in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: There were active people who were working. We were just in the reserve force. So what does that mean? What does reserve force mean? That means that in case there is an elementary disaster, emergency situations, and our emergency situation precisely was what happened, happened. And so that's how the squad was disbanded, because it was multi-ethnic, and it ceased working, and it no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember: Who was the chief at the detachment of the state security service in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: As far as name and surname is concerned, I cannot remember. He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic? Nothing. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Erletic, for giving evidence again this time. We are finished with you. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the next witness enters the court, do I have any limitations with regard to the examination-in-chief of next witness? He was neither 92 nor 71 witness, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This witness, it has been said before by the Trial Chamber that he's replacing Mr. Krajisnik, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So he's limited to what Mr. Krajisnik was supposed to discuss and in particular variant A and B. So the limitation was 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the activities of SDS party. I gave the proofing notes to my learned friend prior to his testimony, and also yesterday I spoke with my learned friend Mr. Weiner. So in this scope, we shall discuss the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying. You gave the summary --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Summary, yeah, proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe that my learned friend can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. We spoke last night, and he provided extensive summary notes. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, we can proceed. Can the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Would you please introduce yourself for the sake of the record and tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Stanko Pivasevic. I was born on the 31st of August, 1965. I live in Samac and I am a doctor by profession, a doctor of medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pivasevic. Due to the manner of proceeding and the work of the interpreters, as we speak the same language, I would like to ask you to speak a little slower so the interpreters can keep up and so that the record can be taken properly. So speak the way you speak when you're speaking in the parliament of Republika Srpska, in a measured -- at a measured pace. Thank you. Dr. Pivasevic, you are also a member of the parliament of Republika Srpska; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a member of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska. I was elected to parliament at the last parliamentary elections, in October 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And were you also a member of parliament before this period, or rather, a deputy, in the National Assembly of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the first multiparty elections held after the war, in July 1996, I was elected to the parliament of Republika Srpska, and at the extraordinary parliamentary elections in 1997, I was also elected to the parliament of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At present, you are the president of the municipal board of the SDS in Samac; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was elected to this post in March 2002, after the internal party elections that were held on the territory of the municipality of Samac within the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were one of the members of the steering committee for the establishment of the SDS party in 1992; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This party, at the time, had a platform linked to the SDS party of Dr. Jovan Raskovic from the Krajina; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The SDS of the Krajina was established long before the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Dr. Jovan Raskovic was very popular with his Gandhi-like methods of political struggle and he won a great many followers so that there was an initiative to establish the same kind of party in Bosnia, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, following the model of the SDS party established by Dr. Raskovic in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was Dr. Blagoje Simic also a member of the steering committee in the summer of 1990? I'm referring to the steering committee for the founding of the SDS at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: In July 1990, after St. Peter's day, or rather, the 12th of July, when the SDS of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established, several hundred people rallied in Slatina, which is on the territory of the municipality of Samac, wishing to establish the Serbian Democratic Party. Dr. Simic was not a member of the steering committee at that time. I was to meet him for the first time when the steering committee was established in his native village of Kruskovo Polje. That is the steering committee of the SDS for Kruskovo Polje. When Dr. Simic joined the Serbian Democratic Party, this was the first time we met. Later on, in 1990, on the 28th of August, the steering committee of the SDS of the Samac municipality grew into the SDS at the founding -- or constituent assembly, which was held in the village of Obudovac, belonging to the municipality of Samac and which was attended by 10.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And was this rally attended by anyone from the top leadership of the SDS at the republican level?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Almost the entire leadership of the then SDS of Bosnia and Herzegovina, headed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, the then president of the SDS of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the court: At that time, in the political life of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when municipal committees were being set up - not only of the SDS but also the SDA and the HDZ - was it usual for representatives of the highest party leadership to attend such rallies?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The HDZ and the SDA were established before the SDS in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they already had a well-developed political life before the SDS was established. We were established later than the other parties in the then Bosnia and Herzegovina. And as the elections were approaching, which were to be held in December, we had a very short time in which to organise the political party. Yes, it was usual for the leaders of political parties, other political parties also, to attend these rallies, the rallies where the parties were founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Dr. Pivasevic, was -- did Dr. Karadzic visit Samac in 1991?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember Dr. Karadzic visiting after August, when he was at Obudovac, at the SDS rally. I don't remember that he visited Samac after that, until the beginning of 1995, when the National Assembly was held. I think that in the intervening period, Dr. Karadzic did not visit Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Dr. Pivasevic, tell me, please: Talking about the parliamentary elections for the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1990, did you participate in those elections as a candidate, you personally?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I personally, as a candidate, did take part in these elections. I was at the head of the list for the municipal council for the SDS, for the then two-Chamber parliament. There was a house of municipalities and a house of citizens, and I was at the head of the list for the house of for municipalities. And Mr. Mirko Jovanovic was at the head of the list for house of citizens and the list for the local parliament in Samac was headed by Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you elected to the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina at those elections?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: In the first round of elections --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Dr. Pivasevic, just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mirko Jovanovic elected as a deputy in the BH parliament in 1990?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: No, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was he elected, and how?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: As Mr. Jovanovic was on the list for the house of citizens, I think after the death of one of the deputies in the republican parliament, he filled the empty place. I don't know when this happened precisely, but I know that later on he did become a member of the assembly, taking the place of the gentleman who died, whose name I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Try to remember whether this was between 1991 and 1993 or 1994.

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: It was certainly in that period, but I can't tell you exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Was Stevan Todorovic one of the members of the steering committee for the founding of the SDS in Samac in 1990?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not a member of the steering committee. Whether he was a member of the party, I couldn't tell you, because the party had several thousand members and it was hard to know every party member.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, up until April, you were a member of the Municipal Board of the SDS; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was Stevan Todorovic also a member of the Municipal Board of the SDS with you? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did not attend all the meetings, but I think he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: After the elections of 1990, who participated in the government at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Which parties?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: After the elections of 1990, at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as far as I can remember, the most votes were won by the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ, and they set up the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did this principle also apply to the local assembly?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The same principle applied to the local assembly, and now I'm referring specifically to the municipality of Samac, where the SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA divided power among them, or rather, they set up the government at the local level, at the level of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Within the Municipal Board of the SDS of Samac, did you and your colleagues - I mean the other members - before April 1992, did you draw up some plans about the forcible takeover of power?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, appropriate time for our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We'll take our break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. You continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Pivasevic, before the break we spoke of the establishment of the government at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina and at the local level, on the basis of the results of the elections of 1990. Tell me, please: Was Dr. Blagoje Simic ever a deputy of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: No. Dr. Simic was never a deputy of Republika Srpska. As I have already said, at the first multiparty elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 1990, he was at the head of the list for the local parliament in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mirko Dragic ever a deputy of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska? Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Dr. Pivasevic: How would you describe the events in the republican parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 14th and 15th of October, 1991? Very briefly, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, I was not elected at the elections and was not a member of the assembly at that point of time. But what I know from the media is that there was outvoting of the Serbian deputies in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think it was then, if my memory serves me well, that the Serbian deputies left the assembly. They walked out because of this outvoting, because I think that under constitution at the time, there were three constituent nations and there had to be consensus in order for certain decisions to be adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What decisions are you referring to? Are you referring to decisions affecting the vital interests of the various peoples or other decisions?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: The vital interests of the nations, the peoples. The then structure was conceived in a way very similar to that of today. There were constitutional mechanisms to protect the vital interests of any one nation so that the other two nations could not make decisions detrimental to the third constituent nations, and the three constituent nations then and now were the Muslims, the Croats, and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a little bit, Dr. Pivasevic, please. And tell me: What was the topic of debate at this republican parliament session in October 1991? What was being adopted? What was being debated at the time, and why did the Serbian deputies walk out?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: I think that the topic of debate was Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a sovereign state. It was really a long time ago, so I can't remember the exact dates, but I think the topic was the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I know that the response of the Serbian people in November 1990 was to hold a referendum as to whether we wished to remain in Yugoslavia as a sovereign state or not. I think that was the topic discussed at the parliament session at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the referendum, was it in 1990 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: It was in November 1990. I'm certain of that. I apologise. No. It was 1991. I do apologise. It was a mistake. In 1991, in December -- in 1990, that was when the first multiparty elections were held, and the referendum was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, was the referendum held in 1991, the referendum of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as it was on the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The referendum was held in Bosanski Samac, and a vast number of Serbs voted, but so did members of other ethnic groups, to a lesser extent. I'm referring to the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Dr. Pivasevic, do you know when the National Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina was established, approximately?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in January 1992 that the assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established. I think that was its name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was the republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina promulgated at the same time?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: The National Assembly of Republika Srpska, for short, we know what we are referring to, did it enact any kind of recommendation as to the establishment of Serbian municipalities? Do you know anything about this? Just tell us whether you remember this or not.

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Dr. Pivasevic: Do you know anything about the fact that in late February, or rather, on the 29th of February, the Serbian municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation was established? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Dr. Pivasevic, do you know anything as to whether the constitution of Republika Srpska was adopted in this period, and other legislation?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was adopted then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fact that it was then that the government was established and certain ministries of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Later on in your political life, did you learn that at that time ministries were established and the government of Republika Srpska was set up?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Please don't ask me about the time when this happened and how this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me now whether you know anything about the Serbian Autonomous region of northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: I heard of the autonomous regions of Krajina, Majevica, Semberija, Herzegovina, and also Northern Bosnia, but in practice, this never actually functioned properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, Dr. Pivasevic, what you know about how the Croats organised themselves at that time. Did they also organise certain communities? If you know.

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: I think that sometime in October or November, in the autumn of 1991, the Croatian community of Bosnian Posavina was organised. I don't know the exact date, but I think it was in the autumn, in October or November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And as far as you know, if you do know, did this community also cover the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bosanski Samac is in the heart of Posavina, so this was unavoidable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Dr. Pivasevic, at the Municipal Board of the SDS in October 1991 until April 1992, did you discuss a certain instruction or a document issued by the Main Board of the SDS about the establishment of crisis staffs, the takeover of power, or anything like that? Was there any such discussion?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Not about crisis staffs, but we were preoccupied at the time with the referendum. After January, I think it was in February, an Official Gazette of the assembly of the Serbian people, which was then established, published a recommendation on the establishment of Serbian assemblies at lower levels, and then we discussed the Cutilheiro plan, which was topical at the time, and the Main Board of the SDS, which was in charge of the overall policy of the party, took this down to a lower level, and as far as I know, we discussed the Cutilheiro plan and we supported the Main Board of the party in accepting the Cutilheiro plan, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts in connection with these topics with the SDA and the HDZ at the local level? Was this discussed in inter-party contacts?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, both the HDZ and the SDA accepted the Cutilheiro plan. It was only when Mr. Izetbegovic returned from Lisbon that he withdrew his signature accepting the plan, and we were in some sort of coalition. I don't know. I didn't take part in these negotiations. Because at the local level the HDZ, the SDA, and the SDS took part in the government, there probably were daily contacts among all these people who were in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In February or March 1992, you experienced an incident with members of paramilitary units who were Croats in -- let me just check the name of the village. I think it was Hasici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. At line 37, page 13 -- I'm sorry. Page 37, line 13, he was asked -- the witness was asked a very specific question about what has been referred to as the variant A and B. I didn't object because he didn't answer the question, then I thought there would be a follow-up question or two in relation to that initial question. It has not been answered. And I'd request that -- this is his main purpose to be here, and I'd request that the witness answer it or the question be asked again. Or let the witness say he has no recollection and no knowledge of the issue or the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the purpose of my question, Your Honour, and he said not about crisis staffs. So we all know that the main topic in this alleged document is establishment of crisis staffs. So my question was very precise and also his answer, not about crisis staffs. But we were preoccupied with the other topics. What the witness can say if the answer is negative, if there is no discussions and if there is not any knowledge of that. I don't know how to -- maybe that's an issue for my learned friend in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's much more than crisis staffs. The question has not been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Mr. Pantelic, the point that Mr. Weiner raises, referring to your question on page 37, line 13 -- I mean, you do ask the witness: "At the Municipal Board of the SDS, in October 1991 until April 1992, did you discuss a certain instruction or a document issued by the Main Board of the SDS about the establishment of crisis staffs, the takeover of power, or anything like that? Was there any such discussion?" Maybe you should be putting to the witness Exhibit P3 and asking him whether he's ever seen it. Because obviously --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's why this witness is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That we can -- by this way we can resolve the matter. Of course, Your Honour. I do appreciate your suggestion. So could we have Exhibit P3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, so that we don't waste any time, Dr. Pivasevic: What happened to you personally sometime in February or March 1992, and where?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in March 1992, I set off with a friend of mine. We went to a restaurant. And the two of us, sometime at 9.00 or 10.00 in the evening, between Hasici, where we were going through, we were stopped by some armed persons. From the car I could see that they had HOS on their sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was does that mean, HOS?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: They mean Croatian armed forces. They stopped us. They searched us. And among them I recognised one person from a neighbouring village. And we had a -- we had words, and after about half an hour, they released us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the -- the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: I think his last name was Blazanovic, and I think I heard that he was killed in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What's his nationality?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the colour of the uniform?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: It was at night that it happened, and the only thing I saw was that insignia on the sleeve, because he had his rifle next to the coat driver's window and I saw that sleeve next to the window [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Pivasevic, could you please slow down. Now you will be shown a document. Could you tell me -- first of all, have a look at it. Just have a look at it carefully and slowly. Take your time. Take the time you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I hope, Your Honours, that this time will be deducted from my time limits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you can go and get what you want from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Dr. Pivasevic, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The contents of the document and the topics discussed in the document, did you ever discuss those at the Municipal Board meetings of Samac Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Doctor -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic. I'm wondering if -- the witness -- you've asked him whether he's ever seen the document before, and he says: "No. This is the first time I see it." You've just put it in front of him, or the usher has, two seconds ago, and now you're asking him whether the contents of the document and the topics to be discussed were ever discussed at the Municipal Board meetings, and he immediately answers no, before having had a chance to look through eight pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour, was that he already did that. He was familiarising himself with the content of document, of course not in every word and every point and comment, but in general, and then the answer was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe I can proceed with the other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As long as the witness has had an opportunity, because it seemed to be like a flash that it was put before him, and I'm just wondering, even if one speed reads, there is eight pages' worth here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, maybe we shall take additional time now to discuss that with the witness. Maybe he can familiarise. But shall I proceed with the questions with regard to the topics and then we shall throw our conclusions with regard to the document? Finally my learned friend will have his time for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that's fine, Mr. Pantelic, as long as the witness has in fact familiarised himself. That's just fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Dr. Pivasevic, you've already answered a part of my question, the question I asked earlier. At the local Municipal Board of SDS Samac, was the alleged instruction discussed of the SDS that came from the level of the republic, level of Republika Srpska, how the Serb people should take over the power and, in a specific case, in Samac? Did you discuss that or not?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. This is the first time he see this document. This is the first time I hear this topic, what you've told me. I'm answering decisively: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The following question: At the Municipal Board of the SDS, did you discuss your cooperation, the SDS cooperation and the JNA cooperation at the local level, at the Samac level?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: No. JNA had its own hierarchy, its military structure. In Belgrade they had their own organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Pivasevic, but the local level of the municipal SDS in Samac, Municipal Board of the SDS Samac, did you speak with the JNA in Samac? Did you make joint plans about the takeover of power in Samac?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At the Municipal Board of the SDS, did you make any plans about calling volunteers from Serbia who would take part in the takeover of power in the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me: You were mobilised in the JNA sometime in December or January, so that was December 1991 or January 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was your unit that you were in? Where were you mobilised? In which unit?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: It was anti-tank company of a battalion that was commanded by Captain Subotin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was your unit part of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the 17th Tactical Group was present in that area. That was the area of responsibility of that group, as far as I understand. But I cannot tell you for sure, because I don't know much about the military hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what happened on the 16th of April, 1992, to you, specifically?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1992, sometime in the afternoon hours, there was an active officer of the JNA who came to my unit. His name was Spasoje Sekulic. And he alarmed my unit, that is, and in the evening hours we went to a combat position. That was 600, 700 metres from the bridge on the Sava River. And we were explained, we were told that there were armed -- armoured units coming from the Republic of Croatia. They were supposed to cross the bridge over the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you stay at this position in the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992? Can you tell the answer for the record?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What happened in the early morning hours, 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning on the 17th of April, 1992, in the position where you were?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: At my position specifically, nothing. We just heard -- we heard a noise, because that was very nearby these -- I can't tell you which exactly, which motor vehicles on the other side, but nobody crossed over to that side, to the Bosnian side, and we -- there was no operations that we engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you heard some noise on the Croatian side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your unit, what weapons did it have?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: It had recoilless guns, recoilless cannons, anti-tank cannons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At that time, from the silos position, or thereabouts, was there an exchange of fire between the sides?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know much about weapons, but as far as the people told me who were there, I think there was fire opened from the position of the silos, with some guided missiles, precisely these armoured units that were on the other side of the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: How long did you stay at that position by the bridge?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly. Two or three days until police forces arrived, and they had a checkpoint established on the bridge, and then we were repositioned several kilometres towards Grebnice, in the area of the village of Tursinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was that a front line between the Croatian forces and the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was your duty in that unit?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: I was a soldier, a private in that unit. But because I was about to graduate in medicine, and because I am slightly disabled because of my vision, as you can see, I was mostly looking after the wounded and the sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. How long did you stay on that position on the front line?

utterances.speaker: STANKO PIVASEVIC
utterances.text: Sometime until October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
